prompt: Where is a VPC firewall rule enforced?
hint: There is no box to size.

choices.text: At an appliance at the edge of the network
choices.why: There is no appliance; the rule is part of the network.

choices.text: At each machine's interface
choices.why: Right. Two machines in one subnet are filtered from each other as from the internet.

choices.text: At the subnet's gateway address
choices.why: Traffic inside a subnet would then go unfiltered, and it does not.

choices.text: At the organisation's root node
choices.why: Firewall policies can be attached there; enforcement is at the machine.

prompt: Two rules match a packet: an allow at priority 500 and a deny at priority 1000. What happens?

choices.text: It is denied, since deny always wins
choices.why: Deny wins only at the same priority.

choices.text: It is denied, since 1000 is higher
choices.why: The lower number is read first.

choices.text: Google refuses to create the second rule
choices.why: Rules at different priorities coexist.

choices.text: It is allowed, by the rule at 500
choices.why: Right. 500 is read before 1000, and the first match decides.

prompt: An allow and a deny for the same packet are both at priority 1000. Which decides?

choices.text: The deny, at a tie
choices.why: Right. At the same priority, deny wins.

choices.text: The allow, as the more specific one
choices.why: Specificity is not part of the order.

choices.text: Whichever was created first
choices.why: Creation order is not part of it either.

choices.text: Neither; the implied rule decides
choices.why: The implied rule is only read when nothing above matches.

prompt: A custom mode network has no rules at all. Can one of its machines reach another on port 22?

choices.text: Yes, traffic inside a network is free
choices.why: That was the default network's extra rule, not a property of networks.

choices.text: Yes, the implied rule allows SSH
choices.why: The implied ingress rule denies.

choices.text: No: the implied rule denies all ingress
choices.why: Right. Even traffic between its own machines needs a rule to be allowed in.

choices.text: Only from the same zone
choices.why: Zones do not change firewall rules.

prompt: Why does the planner not use the default network?

choices.text: It has no firewall rules
choices.why: It has four.

choices.text: It cannot have custom rules added
choices.why: Rules can be added to any network.

choices.text: It allows SSH, RDP and ping from anywhere
choices.why: Right. Those three rules open every machine in it to the internet.

choices.text: It denies egress
choices.why: The implied egress rule allows.

prompt: A project administrator writes a priority 0 allow for SSH from anywhere into production. The planner's security team had already decided no SSH from the internet into production. Where must that decision live to hold?

choices.text: A firewall policy on the folder
choices.why: Right. Policies on the tree are evaluated before the network's own rules.

choices.text: A deny at priority 0 in the same network
choices.why: The administrator can delete it; it is their network.

choices.text: The implied deny rule
choices.why: It sits at 65535, below everything.

choices.text: A budget on production
choices.why: Budgets see money, not packets.

prompt: Why can a network tag widen a rule more easily than a service account can?
hint: Who can put each on a machine?

choices.text: Tags apply to every network in the project
choices.why: A rule's tag applies in its own network.

choices.text: Tags are inherited from the folder
choices.why: Network tags are on machines, not on the tree.

choices.text: Service accounts cannot be targets
choices.why: They can, and the planner uses them.

choices.text: Anyone who edits the machine adds tags
choices.why: Right. Attaching an account needs a role on the account itself.

choices.text: The implied rule already uses it
choices.why: The implied rules are at 65535.

choices.text: Priorities stop at 65535
choices.why: Right. The provider checks the range before asking Google.

choices.text: The network has a rule at that priority
choices.why: The plan asked nothing about the network.

choices.text: Priorities must be multiples of 100
choices.why: Any number from 0 to 65535 is accepted.

prompt: The plan reported `source_tags` conflicting with `target_service_accounts`. What is the fix?
hint: One way of naming per rule.

choices.text: Name the web machines by their account
choices.why: Right. A rule names machines by tags or by accounts, never both.

choices.text: Split it into two rules at the same priority
choices.why: Each would still need a source and a target named the same way.

choices.text: Add `direction = "INGRESS"`
choices.why: The direction was not the conflict.

choices.text: Replace the tag with the web machines' addresses
choices.why: That works, and breaks the first time a machine is replaced.

prompt: In the corrected plan, `direction` was *known after apply*. Why?
hint: The file did not say one.

choices.text: Terraform cannot plan directions
choices.why: It plans one when the file states it.

choices.text: The rule is both ingress and egress
choices.why: A rule has one direction.

choices.text: Google fills in INGRESS at creation
choices.why: Right. The direction is set by the API when the file leaves it out.

choices.text: The network does not exist yet
choices.why: The priority was known though the network was not.

prompt: A firewall rule with no priority written gets priority ___.
Why does the planner's `rules.json` have no rule saying *deny everything else*?

choices.text: JSON cannot express a deny
choices.why: The last rule is a deny.

choices.text: The implied deny ingress already does it
choices.why: Right. Anything no rule allows in is refused at 65535.

choices.text: Google forbids catch-all denies
choices.why: They are allowed; they are redundant here.

choices.text: The health checks would fail
choices.why: Not at a lower precedence than their allow.

prompt: SSH from 35.235.240.7 to a web machine tagged `frozen` matches `allow-ssh-from-iap` at 1000 and `deny-ssh-to-frozen` at 900. What decides?

choices.text: The allow, written earlier in the file
choices.why: The file's order means nothing; priority does.

choices.text: Both, so the packet is half allowed
choices.why: One rule decides.

choices.text: The implied rule, after a conflict
choices.why: There is no conflict; the order settles it.

choices.text: The deny, read first at 900
choices.why: Right. The allow at 1000 is never reached.

prompt: The reports job was refused by the database. What fix does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: A source range of 10.0.0.0/8 on allow-web-to-db
choices.why: That opens the database to every machine in the network.

choices.text: Running the reports job as web@
choices.why: That gives it every permission web@ holds.

choices.text: Deleting the implied deny
choices.why: It cannot be deleted.

choices.text: A rule naming reports as a source
choices.why: Right. Written and reviewed like the others.

prompt: At what priority did `walk.py` say the implied rule decided?
Match each source range in rules.json to what sends from it.
Put the steps Google takes for one packet in order.
items: firewall policies on the organisation and folders
the network's rules, lowest number first
at a tie, deny before allow
trap: Reading the network's rules first is the slip: a policy on the tree is evaluated before them, which is how it holds against a project's own priority 0.

prompt: The planner wants machines kept for an investigation to be unreachable by SSH, whoever edits them. Which rule fits, and why is a tag acceptable here?
hint: What can a misplaced tag do?

choices.text: An allow at 900 on tag frozen, from IAP
choices.why: That opens SSH, the opposite of the aim.

choices.text: A deny at 900 on tag frozen; a stray tag closes, never opens
choices.why: Right. A tag that takes access away makes a machine harder to reach, nothing more.

choices.text: A deny at 70000, below the implied rule
choices.why: Priorities stop at 65535, and below the allows it would never be read.

choices.text: Removing the machines' service accounts
choices.why: allow-ssh-from-iap targets all machines; removing an account changes nothing for it.
